title: The death of the brave
hook: death is the right of the brave, if it is accepted in the Lord's court (Vadhans M1, ang 579)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alaahnee, and your line: all must go. Did you tell someone one thing you're glad about in them? Today, the next lament asks a harder question: if all must go, how? Day six hundred seventy-five.

People who work in hospice sometimes say the same thing: there's a difference between someone who dies afraid and someone who dies ready. Not braver in the movie sense. Just settled. They've said what they needed to say. They've made their peace. Most of us don't like to think about it at all. We change the subject, knock on wood, scroll past. Guru Nanak's second lament doesn't change the subject. It says there's such a thing as a good death, and it says who gets one. Today: the death of the brave.
screen: `DYING AFRAID, OR DYING READY.` → `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `A LAMENT THAT DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: The second of Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, on Ang five seventy-nine, has a line Sikhs know well. In paraphrase: death is the right of the brave, of true heroes, if their death is accepted. And nearby: don't call death bad, people, if one knows how to truly die. The word for the brave is sooraa, a hero, a warrior. But look who the hymn says the heroes are. In paraphrase again: they alone are called brave who receive honor in the true court. They leave with honor, and are honored when they arrive. So bravery here isn't measured by the battlefield. It's measured by acceptance in the dargah, the Lord's court. What makes a death accepted? The hymn's answer, and the Granth's answer everywhere, is a life lived remembering the Name, serving, honest. The death of the brave is the end of a brave life: one that didn't flinch from truth. That's why these lines mean so much to a community with many martyrs. Sikhs remember Guru Arjan, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's sons, and countless others who faced death without giving up their faith. But the hymn belongs just as much to a grandmother dying in her bed, having lived kindly and remembered God. Her death, too, is the death of the brave. One more word: parvaan, accepted, approved, signed off. It's the key to the line. The question isn't how you die. It's whether the life it ends is accepted.
screen: `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD.` · `SOORAA: WHO THE BRAVE ARE.` · `HONORED IN THE TRUE COURT.` · `PARVAAN: ACCEPTED.` · then, large: `ACCEPTED IN HIS COURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live one brave hour. Sit, and think of the next hour of your day. What would it look like lived bravely, in this hymn's sense? Not dramatic. Just true: the honest answer, the patient word, the thing you've been avoiding. Choose one. Picture yourself doing it calmly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and ask to live this hour in a way that would be accepted. The bell holds the time.
The death of the brave. Guru Nanak's lament: death is the right of the brave, if it's accepted in the Lord's court; don't call death bad, if one knows how truly to die.
screen: `THE DEATH OF THE BRAVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: accepted in his court. Today, do one brave, true thing in a single hour, and let that hour be enough. Day six hundred seventy-five.

screen: `DAY 675 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SHABAD FOR YOUR HOME.`

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa at funerals and remembrances, and these lines on the death of the brave are often recalled when martyrs are remembered.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a hero, a brave one; in the lament, the brave are those accepted in the court.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a hymn praising death in battle.
what it means: a good death is the end of a true life, accepted in God's court, for anyone.
what a scholar hears: the lament turns the martial word sooraa toward parvaan, acceptance in the dargah, the Granth's measure of a life.
